result.title: Preface
result.summary: The District of Columbia Retirement Board’s January 10, 2011 RFP seeks a real-assets investment consultant (DCRB-2011-001). Letters of interest are due January 21, questions January 28, and proposals February 25, all at 5 p.m. EST; firms receiving it elsewhere must contact the procurement officer to receive updates. The RFP covers background, scope, agreement term, proposal requirements, selection, timetable, minimum criteria, and attachments on warranties, questionnaires, fees, fiduciary definitions, bonding, service providers, and current managers. The Board, an independent agency managing police, firefighters’ and teachers’ retirement funds, seeks prudent investment advice, implementation support, strategy and manager evaluation, and education. It describes Board governance, advisers, and a search authorized in 2010; incumbent Townsend and general consultant Meketa are expected to compete. At September 2010, assets exceeded $4.2 billion, with specified allocation targets and real-assets holdings and commitments. Required services include strategic advice, research, meetings and coordination; manager sourcing, due diligence, recommendations and contract negotiations; and timely monitoring of portfolio events.

result.title: Real Assets Consulting, Sourcing, and Due Diligence
key_items: B. Deal Sourcing and Due Diligence
result.summary: The Board seeks an experienced public-fund consultant to advise its real assets portfolio, work closely with Staff, and report regularly to the Investment Committee. Strategic services include recurring policy, objectives, and strategy recommendations; requested research, analyses, risk monitoring, and cash-flow and commitment-pacing models; advice on investment issues and special projects; presentations and responses at Board, committee, and other meetings; counsel to Staff; ongoing coordination with portfolio stakeholders; and related consulting. The Consultant and Staff will jointly source managers through a structured search of available investments, including detailed analysis of Staff-identified prospects. For prospects selected by the Investment Committee, the Consultant will conduct due diligence, including review of compliance with pension-fund laws. Written recommendations to the Committee and Staff must cover due-diligence findings, strategic considerations, portfolio fit, and legal and economic terms. The Consultant will also support Staff and legal counsel in negotiating contracts.

result.title: C. Monitoring of the Real Assets Portfolio
result.summary:
C. Monitoring of the Real Assets Portfolio
In monitoring the portfolio, the Consultant must:
1. Take responsibility for the timely review and analysis of key events that may affect the real assets portfolio. Key events could include market changes, changes in management
5or substantial changes in portfolio value. 2. Assist in actions taken to protect the interests of the Board as an investor and interact, where necessary, with portfolio investment advisers and funds to ensure compliance by each with contract terms. 3. Assist in attending partnership annual meetings, and, where appropriate, serve on advisory boards and report back to the Board and Staff. 4. Review and recommend courses of action for all fund document amendments.

result.title: D. Performance Measurement and Reporting
result.summary: The Consultant will collect monthly and/or quarterly real asset investment data from managers, verify its accuracy against custodian records, and calculate US-dollar returns, reconciling performance and currency conversions with partner and manager reports. Time- and dollar-weighted returns will be reported for individual partnerships, asset classes, and the total portfolio. Reports will analyze diversification by risk profile, property type, geography, and Board-defined risk mitigants. A customized quarterly report will include a global market update; fund organizational and portfolio updates; commitment dates and amounts, total commitments, drawdowns, outstanding commitments, distributions, NAVs, net investment multiples, net IRRs, and relevant benchmarks. Commitment through benchmark data will also be aggregated by asset class and for the overall portfolio, with allocations broken down by vintage year, strategy, property type, and geography.

result.title: E. Other
result.summary: The Consultant will provide Board/Staff workshops on designated or recommended issues; analyze proposed federal and state legislation affecting the real assets portfolio; support Staff, the Board, or Investment Committee through written or oral presentations to government agencies, legislative committees, auditors, and others; and meet quarterly with Staff to review the portfolio, discuss market conditions and new issues, and recommend improvements. The original agreement lasts three years. Proposal instructions must be followed or a proposal may be disqualified. Submissions become Board property and may be publicly disclosed under FOIA; proprietary or confidential information must be identified. Interested firms must send signed originals of a letter of interest with follow-up contact details, the signed Representation and Warranties (Attachment A), and documentation for the Minimum Criteria (Section 8.0) to the D.C. Retirement Board, Attn: Yolanda Smith, 900 7th Street N.W., Suite 200, Washington, D.C. 20001, by 5:00 p.m. EST January 21, 2011. Late or incomplete submissions are excluded. RFP questions must be emailed by 5:00 p.m. January 28, 2011 to realassets.rfp@dc.gov.

result.title: Agreement Term and Proposal Submission Requirements
key_items: 5.2 Letter of Interest / Representation & Warranties Submission
result.summary: The consultant must support the Board and Investment Committee through presentations to agencies, committees, and auditors, and meet quarterly with Staff to review the real assets portfolio, discuss market conditions and issues, and recommend improvements. The Agreement lasts three years. Proposal instructions must be followed or an offer may be disqualified; submissions become Board property and may be publicly disclosed, so proprietary or confidential information must be identified. Interested firms must submit signed originals of a letter of interest with contact details, the Representation and Warranties form, and documentation addressing the minimum criteria. Send them to Yolanda Smith at the D.C. Retirement Board, 900 7th Street, N.W., Suite 200, Washington, D.C. 20001, by 5:00 p.m. EST, Friday, January 21, 2011. Late or incomplete submissions are excluded from further consideration.

result.title: 5.3 Inquiries
result.summary: RFP questions must be emailed by 5:00 p.m. January 28, 2011; written answers and the questions will be posted on the DCRB website. Proposals, including all attachments, are due by 5:00 p.m. February 25, 2011; late, faxed, or emailed submissions are not accepted. Submit one original and eight copies (one unbound), plus a USB drive with the complete electronic response, to Yolanda Smith at the D.C. Retirement Board, 900 7th Street NW, Suite 200, Washington, DC 20001. Proposals must include an authorized, signed cover letter with representative contact details; complete questionnaire responses reproducing each question before its answer; a completed, signed fee schedule; and the firm’s latest Form ADV, Parts I and II. Responses, including fees, are public records under D.C. FOIA. Firms bear all proposal and related costs, including travel.

result.title: Proposal Submission, Public Records, and Costs
result.summary: Inquiries and responses will be provided in writing and posted on the DCRB website. Proposals, including all attachments, must arrive by 5:00 p.m. February 25, 2011; late, faxed, or emailed submissions will not be accepted. Offerors must send the original and eight copies (one unbound), plus a USB drive with the complete electronic response, to Yolanda Smith at the D.C. Retirement Board’s listed address. Proposals must include an authorized, signed cover letter with representative contact details; complete, succinct questionnaire responses that repeat each question; a completed, signed fee schedule; and the firm’s latest Form ADV, Parts I and II. All responses, including fees, are public records under the D.C. Freedom of Information Act. Each firm bears its submission and related costs, including travel.

result.title: Proposal Withdrawal and Consultant Selection
result.summary: Firms may withdraw submitted responses in writing before the deadline. During the selection period, RFP recipients must avoid unauthorized contact with Board trustees or staff, except for ordinary necessary business or public-record matters. The Board may award based on written responses without negotiation or end the process without selecting or notifying firms. Before agreement execution, it may amend or rescind terms and request supplemental information. Investment Staff select interview finalists; the Investment Committee interviews them at the Board office and recommends a choice for Board approval. The Board seeks the highest-quality consultant through an open, fair, competitive process and retains sole award discretion. Staff evaluate applicants on scope understanding, firm experience and resources, consultant qualifications, conflicts of interest, and fees, each weighted 20%.

result.title: 8.0 Minimum Criteria
key_items: 8.7 The firm is not involved in pending litigation or under a censure or restraining order by a court of proper jurisdiction or in bankruptcy, conservatorship, or receivership.
8.8 The firm will disclose any legal and/or regulatory inquiries and/or sanctions against the firm or any individuals employed by the firm.
8.9 The firm will carry adequate fiduciary liability insurance, errors & omissions insurance, and fidelity bond insurance.
8.10 The firm agrees to disclose all conflicts of interest, all sources of revenue and all affiliations.
result.summary: The RFP requires firms to satisfy all minimum criteria or face immediate rejection: be a registered investment adviser and submit current Form ADV Parts I and II; hold all required authorizations; agree to fiduciary duties under ERISA and D.C. law; accept the specified representations and warranties for incorporation into a contract; have at least five years’ experience advising three U.S. public pension funds with at least $5 billion each; and assign a 10-year-experienced senior consultant who becomes knowledgeable about the portfolio, reports clearly, attends meetings, and cannot be replaced without Board approval. Firms must not be in litigation, under censure or restraining order, or in insolvency proceedings; disclose inquiries, sanctions, conflicts, revenues, and affiliations; and maintain adequate fiduciary, errors-and-omissions, and fidelity-bond insurance. Attachment A requires an executed warranty statement covering bonding or exemption, E&O coverage, lawful and prudent performance, required regulatory filings and approvals, compliance with minimum criteria, and signer authority, with firm and signature details. Attachment B is the proposal questionnaire.

result.title: A. Organizational Background
result.summary: Requests organizational and contact details for the firm; its history, founding year, ownership structure, parent/affiliate/joint venture relationships, owners’ percentages and biographies, and past or anticipated ownership, structural, or staffing changes. Seeks years of real assets consulting experience overall and with public pension funds, plus the share of revenue from these services. Requests current-client totals and aggregate assets; public pension client counts and assets under advisement; client-category percentages; distributions by asset-size range and geographic region. Also asks for details on real assets consulting relationships terminated or gained since January 1, 2008, including counts, client names, asset values, reasons for terminations, and contact persons’ names, positions, and telephone numbers.

result.title: B. Professional Staff
result.summary: Requests information on the firm’s professional organization, including an organizational chart, staff functions and names, and totals for professional and support employees. Seeks profiles of dedicated real assets researchers and all professionals assigned to the Board’s account, including designated primary and secondary consultants, qualifications, experience, tenure, current clients and asset sizes, and office locations. For those clients, requests reference contact details and asset sizes. Also asks how the Board’s team operates and provides coverage when consultants are unavailable; professional staff turnover since January 1, 2008, with names, positions, departure dates, and reasons; average clients per consultant (excluding primarily research-focused consultants); professional compensation and incentive-bonus arrangements; and plans for growth in real assets investment consulting.

result.title: C. Services and Capabilities
result.summary: The questionnaire covers the firm’s consulting and financial services, business lines and revenue/profit contributions, real assets research structure, and investment beliefs. It asks how the firm sets and adjusts real assets allocations, selects benchmarks, compares portfolios, and maintains manager-performance databases. It seeks international and emerging-markets expertise; manager evaluation, due diligence, monitoring, search experience, alpha identification, competitive advantages, access to constrained funds, and criteria and timelines for watchlisting or replacing managers. It also addresses performance measurement, data verification, reporting teams and sample reports, benchmarks and universe robustness. Respondents must describe notable client recommendations and value added, a challenging public pension issue and its outcome, views on active versus passive strategies, key pension-fund risks and their management, and experience educating trustees and staff.

result.title: D. Legal Issues and Potential Conflicts
result.summary: The text requests disclosures about SEC investment-adviser registration and examination reports; ERISA and D.C. law fiduciary commitments; Form ADV filings; relevant litigation, investigations, or regulatory proceedings; insurance coverage and carriers; and contractual liability limits. It asks firms to identify potential conflicts, relationships with D.C. government or employee organizations, roles with Fund fiduciaries or providers, money-management activities, broker-dealer status and trading, soft-dollar practices, ownership interests, manager-related fees, sales of databases or performance analytics, and other manager compensation, including conflict controls. It also asks about limits on Board use of consulting materials and requires the firm’s ethics and conflicts policies. The fee schedule requires annual bundled fees for all scope-of-work services, including travel and other expenses, with any excluded required services identified. Fees must be guaranteed for at least three years; negotiated fees cannot exceed the proposal. Year 1–3 fees, total, firm and signatory names, date, and signature are requested.

result.title: District of Columbia Retirement Board Request for Proposal Real Assets Investment Consulting Services Fiduciary Definition under D.C. Retirement Reform Act
result.summary: The section defines fiduciaries under the D.C. Retirement Reform Act to include those exercising control over Fund assets, providing compensated investment advice, or bearing related authority or administrative responsibility. The Board, its members, and designated fiduciaries must act solely for participants and beneficiaries, prudently and diligently, diversify investments unless imprudent, and follow governing law and documents; the Board retains prudent oversight when designating others. Fiduciaries and persons handling Fund property generally must be bonded, subject to specified supervised-corporation exemptions and conditions for certain trust institutions. Bonds are generally set at the lesser of 10% of funds handled or $500,000, with a $1,000 minimum, and must protect against fraud or dishonesty, use approved forms and sureties, and avoid conflicted providers. The Mayor may waive the cap after notice and hearing; handling property unbonded is unlawful, and the Council must issue regulations. The section also provides statutory credits, codification history, a repealed statutory reference, and the cited D.C. Code’s currency date.

nodes.title: § 1-741. Fiduciary Responsibilities.
nodes.summary: The excerpt from the D.C. Retirement Board’s real-assets investment consulting RFP defines a fiduciary as a person who exercises discretionary control over a Fund or its assets, provides compensated investment advice, or has related authority or responsibility, including in Fund administration. The Board, its members, and defined fiduciaries must act as fiduciaries; the Board may designate others but retains a duty of careful, prudent oversight. Fiduciaries must act solely for participants’ and beneficiaries’ interests and exclusively to provide benefits, using prudent care, skill, and diligence; diversify investments to limit large-loss risk unless clearly imprudent; and follow governing laws and documents insofar as consistent with the chapter. The excerpt also introduces a Bonding Requirement attachment.

nodes.title: § 1-745. Bonding.
nodes.summary: Fund fiduciaries and anyone handling Fund property must be bonded, except qualifying U.S. or state corporations authorized for trust or insurance business, subject to government supervision, and maintaining capital and surplus above a Council-set minimum of at least $1 million. Non-FDIC-insured trust institutions qualify only if they meet state bonding requirements deemed equivalent to federal bank requirements. Bonds are generally the lesser of 10% of funds handled or $500,000, with a $1,000 minimum; the Mayor may waive the cap after notice and hearing. Amounts are set each fiscal year based on the prior reporting year’s funds handled, including predecessors, or estimates for a new Fund. Bonds must protect against fraud or dishonesty, use Council-approved forms, and be backed by an approved corporate surety. Handling Fund property while unbonded, or permitting it, is unlawful. Bonds may not be obtained from providers with significant Fund-related interests. No other law requires additional bonding for such Fund handling, and the Council must issue implementing regulations.
